title: Taste apart, adjust together
allegory: Data-parallel training is like a team of cooks with identical recipe books, each tasting a different tray from the same batch, who phone in and average their suggested tweaks so every book gets exactly the same edit.
map: a cook with an identical recipe book
a GPU process holding a full model replica
each cook's own tray of spoonfuls
that rank's slice of the batch (batch_size / N)
the local gradient on that slice
the phone call that averages every tweak
everyone copies the head cook's book on day one
broadcast param.data from rank 0 at init

cap.1: Training tastes thousands of examples per step. One cook with one spoon takes forever. Could eight cooks share the work without their recipes drifting apart?
cap.2: One GPU can only push so many examples through forward and backward per second. Data parallelism puts a full copy of the model on each GPU and splits every batch between them.
cap.3: Data parallelism: N replicas, each on batch_size/N examples. Model parallelism (tensor or pipeline) splits the model itself instead; you need it only once a model no longer fits on one GPU.

cap.1: Every cook gets an identical recipe book and a different tray of spoonfuls. Each tastes their own tray and writes down how they'd tweak the recipe.
cap.2: Each rank runs forward and backward on its own sub-batch, independently. DistributedSampler hands every rank a disjoint slice; call set_epoch(epoch) so the shuffle changes each epoch.
cap.3: Per-rank gradients are estimates from disjoint sub-batches. Replicas must start bit-identical: broadcast param.data from rank 0 at init, because the collectives take plain tensors, not nn.Parameters.

cap.1: Then everyone phones in their tweak, the tweaks are averaged, and every cook gets the same average back. Same start, same update: the recipes never drift.
cap.2: all_reduce sums each parameter's .grad across ranks and leaves the result on every rank; divide by world_size to average. Then every rank steps its optimizer and the replicas stay identical.
cap.3: With equal disjoint sub-batches, the mean of per-rank mean gradients is exactly the full-batch gradient. ARENA builds all_reduce from send/recv (gather, then broadcast); ring all-reduce avoids the root bottleneck.

chapters.name: Same clock, worse score
chapters.verdict: Four GPUs, same wall clock, worse accuracy? Check the divide and the sampler.

cap.1: Two classic slips: the cooks add up their tweaks instead of averaging, or they all taste the very same tray. Either way, extra cooks buy you nothing.
cap.2: Forgot ÷ world_size? Every gradient is 4x too big: an effective LR of 4x, worse accuracy, no divergence. Plain DataLoader on each rank? All four do the same examples: 4x the work, no speedup.
cap.3: SUM without the divide scales the effective LR by world_size; a non-distributed loader makes N gradients N copies of one. Check one param's grad matches across ranks and equals the single-GPU grad on the combined batch.

curves.label: 8x the batch: 8x the LR, warmed up

cap.1: More cooks means a bigger combined tray and a better guess at the right tweak, so you can take a bigger step. But not on day one: ease into it.
cap.2: Goyal et al. (2017) trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet in one hour: batch 8192 on 256 GPUs, no accuracy lost. Their rules: scale the LR linearly with batch size, and warm it up gradually over the first five epochs.
cap.3: Linear scaling rests on the bigger batch's lower-variance gradient; warmup is needed because that assumption fails early, while the network changes fastest. They reported ~90% scaling efficiency from 8 to 256 GPUs.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Batch size and learning rate move together
The big models you'll study were trained this way

cap.1: You'll rarely write this yourself: a library wraps it in one line. Keep the picture, and the rule that batch size and step size move together.
cap.2: PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel does the broadcast and gradient all-reduce for you. Knowing the four changes lets you debug a run that is slow or oddly worse.
cap.3: DDP is a library call; what you keep is averaged gradients = full-batch gradient, and LR-batch coupling. Large models you'll probe and steer are trained this way, usually combined with model parallelism.

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: !reduce ? 'not averaged yet' : (!sampler ? 'wasted: four copies of one slice' : (!divide ? 'summed, not averaged: LR effectively 4x' : 'correct: equals the full-batch gradient'))

caption.1: Switch all_reduce on and watch four different opinions become one. Then switch off the divide, or the sampler, and see each classic bug appear.
caption.2: Correct run: sampler on, sum then ÷ world_size, and every rank holds 0.50, what one GPU gets on the whole batch. No divide: 4x too big. No sampler: four copies of one slice's opinion.
caption.3: The mean of per-rank mean gradients over equal disjoint slices is exactly the full-batch gradient. Summing scales the effective LR by world_size; duplicated data averages N copies of one estimate.

where_else: Gradient accumulation: several small batches on one GPU, averaged before one step (the same maths, spread over time instead of GPUs)
Federated averaging: devices train on their own data and a server averages the updates
Every large training run, combined with tensor and pipeline parallelism once the model outgrows one GPU

hamming.what: Run identical model copies on different slices of each batch and average their gradients so every copy takes the same step.
hamming.when: When one GPU is too slow for your data but the model still fits on a single GPU.
hamming.why: N GPUs act like one bigger batch with four small additions to an unchanged training loop, which is how large models get trained in reasonable time.

object.title: The pin board of gradients
object.subtitle: Four rows of pins, one per GPU; pull the all-reduce lever and every row snaps to the same shape.

cap.1: Four GPUs, four rows of pins. Each row is one GPU's suggested nudge for six weights, worked out from its own slice of the batch.
cap.2: Rows are ranks, columns are parameters, pin height is that rank's local gradient before any communication.
cap.3: Per-rank gradients from disjoint sub-batches: unbiased but noisy estimates of the full-batch gradient.

cap.1: From the front the rows clearly disagree: each slice of data tells a slightly different story.
cap.2: If each rank stepped on its own gradient now, the four replicas would drift apart after one update.
cap.3: Unsynchronised local steps would desynchronise the replicas; data parallelism forbids that by construction.

cap.1: Pull the all-reduce lever: every row snaps to the same profile, the average. Now every GPU takes the identical step.
cap.2: After all_reduce and the divide, every rank holds the column mean, which equals the gradient one GPU would get on the whole batch.
cap.3: The column mean over equal disjoint slices is exactly the full-batch mean-loss gradient, so N replicas stepping on it equal one big-batch model.

cap.1: Forget to divide and every pin is four times too tall. The model still trains, just with steps four times bigger than you asked for.
cap.2: all_reduce sums. Without ÷ world_size the effective learning rate is 4x: accuracy degrades quietly and nothing diverges to warn you.
cap.3: SUM-reduced gradients scale the effective LR by world_size, a silent hyperparameter change rather than a crash.

cap.1: From above all four rows match. Same start, same update, every step: the copies stay identical forever.
cap.2: Identical updates keep identical models identical, which is why the weights are broadcast from rank 0 at the very start.
cap.3: Replica consistency is an invariant: bit-identical init (broadcast) plus identical reduced updates.

predict.q: After all_reduce and the divide, what does each GPU hold?

options.t: The same averaged gradient on every GPU

predict.why: all_reduce leaves the aggregate on every rank; dividing by world_size turns the sum into the average.

predict.q: A 4-GPU run is no faster than 1 GPU and a little less accurate. Most likely cause?

options.t: No DistributedSampler, and no divide by world_size

predict.why: Without a sampler every rank repeats the same work; without the divide the effective learning rate is 4x.

predict.q: Why broadcast the weights from rank 0 before training starts?

options.t: Averaging only keeps copies identical if they start identical

predict.why: Identical updates on different starting weights still leave different models.

object.where: Anywhere many workers compute on different data and must agree on one update: data parallelism, gradient accumulation, federated averaging.
